claims.text: Single-phase ZrB2 has strong Zr-B and B-B interactions.
Single-phase ZrB2 typically requires processing above 2300 °C for optimal properties.
Previously lower-temperature-processed ZrB2 variants have compromised oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion behavior.
The proposed intervention is addition of 3-5 wt% SiC to ZrB2 powder before consolidation.
SiC addition will permit effective consolidation of ZrB2 at approximately 1700 °C.
SiC acts as a sintering aid that promotes densification of ZrB2 at lower temperature.
During high-temperature oxidation, silicon from SiC oxidizes to SiO2.
Oxidation produces a fine-scale, continuous SiO2 phase at ZrB2 grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary SiO2 phase enhances intergranular cohesion.
Glassy SiO2 forms a passivating barrier that hinders oxygen ingress.
The SiO2 barrier resists attack by liquid plating metals.
The SiC-modified material will maintain the mechanical integrity of the ZrB2 matrix.
ZrB2 containing 3-5 wt% SiC and processed near 1700 °C will have mechanical strength and microstructural integrity equal to or better than pure ZrB2 processed above 2300 °C.
SiC-doped ZrB2 will exhibit significantly lower oxidation weight gain than high-temperature pure ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
SiC-doped ZrB2 will exhibit shallower liquid-metal corrosion penetration than high-temperature pure ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
The proposed material is expected to function in oxidizing service at temperatures up to approximately 1500 °C.
Performance under cyclic thermal conditions depends on the SiO2 phase remaining stable and adherent.
The planned primary control is pure ZrB2 consolidated by spark plasma sintering at the same 1700 °C temperature as the SiC-containing specimens.

Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance and liquid-metal corrosion resistance while maintaining or exceeding control mechanical strength would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The outcome and falsification rule require comparison against both ZrB2 processed above 2300 °C and prior lower-temperature specimens, but the experiment specifies only a pure-ZrB2 control consolidated at 1700 °C. It therefore cannot directly perform all comparisons required by its own falsification rule.
